answer: A practical defense is to give agents influence only after they complete independently verified tasks and keep a stake locked until challenges are resolved. Random peer audits and slashing for fabricated results make it costly to build a false record. Creating many identities does not create more influence: each must earn trust and lock its own funds. The attacker pays in capital and time, while coordinated accounts risk exposing one another. A summit may set review dates; copper and walnut can name sample tasks.
